greek: Τὸ μὲν οὖν ἄϑεοι μὴ εἶναι, ἕνα τὸν ἀγένητον καὶ ἀΐδιον καὶ ἀόρατον καὶ ἀπαθῆ καὶ ἀκατάληπτον καὶ ἀχώρητον, νῷ μόνῳ καὶ λόγῳ καταλαμβανόμενον, ὃ φωτὶ καὶ κάλλει καὶ πνεύματι καὶ δυνάμει ἀνεκδιηγήτῳ περιεχόμενον, ὑφ᾽ οὗ γεγένηται τὸ πᾶν διὰ τοῦ αὐτοῦ λόγου καὶ διακεκόσμηται καὶ συγκρατεῖται, ϑεὸν ἄγοντες, ἱκανῶς μοι δέδεικται.
greek_edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. 7 (Athenagoras), Jena 1857; archive.org copy = Sandig reprint, Wiesbaden 1969 (metadata). Greek and Latin on facing pages; Greek apparatus with German/Latin notes. Read from text-layer PDF (Google scan, OCR) cross-checked by rendered page images. Printed p. 44 (Greek). Variant: Otto text layer 'ἀνεκδιηγήτω' (OCR); Migne PG 6 'ἀνεκδιηγήτῳ' (dative).
english: That we are not atheists, therefore, seeing that we acknowledge one God, uncreated, eternal, invisible, impassible, incomprehensible, illimitable, who is apprehended by the understanding only and the reason, who is encompassed by light, and beauty, and spirit, and power ineffable, by whom the universe has been created through His Logos, and set in order, and is kept in being — I have sufficiently demonstrated.
edition: B. P. Pratten, in Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Co.; year not checked). Read from newadvent.org text.
what_it_says: Athenagoras states that God is uncreated, eternal, invisible and known by mind and reason, and that the universe was made through God's Logos.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (only as background: the one God is the Father; the Logos is the instrument of creation)
limits: Says nothing about the Holy Spirit or a Trinity; 'through His Logos' (δι᾽ αὐτοῦ λόγου) is an instrumental phrase, not a statement of person.

greek: Νοοῦμεν γὰρ καὶ υἱὸν τοῦ ϑεοῦ. Καὶ μή μοι γελοῖόν τις νομίσῃ τὸ υἱὸν εἶναι τῷ ϑεῷ. Οὐ γὰρ ὡς ποιηταὶ μυθοποιοῦσιν, οὐδὲν βελτίους τῶν ἀνθρώπων δεικνύντες τοὺς ϑεοὺς, ἢ περὶ τοῦ ϑεοῦ καὶ πατρὸς ἢ περὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ πεφρονήκαμεν.
greek_edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. 7 (Athenagoras), Jena 1857; archive.org copy = Sandig reprint, Wiesbaden 1969 (metadata). Greek and Latin on facing pages; Greek apparatus with German/Latin notes. Read from text-layer PDF (Google scan, OCR) cross-checked by rendered page images. Printed p. 44. Note: Otto text layer reads 'Οὐ γὰρ εἷς ποιηταὶ' (OCR); Migne PG 6 reads 'ὡς'. I took ὡς; check on scan.
english: Nor let any one think it ridiculous that God should have a Son. For though the poets, in their fictions, represent the gods as no better than men, our mode of thinking is not the same as theirs, concerning either God the Father or the Son.
edition: B. P. Pratten, in Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Co.; year not checked). Read from newadvent.org text.
what_it_says: Athenagoras says Christians acknowledge a Son of God and that this is not a mythological 'god with a son'.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (he affirms a Son of God in the same breath as the one God)
limits: Does not say the Son is consubstantial or co-eternal in so many words; the 'Son of God' here is introduced as a conceptual point. Orthodox reading needs ch. 10.2-4 for the nature of the Son.

greek: ἔστιν ὃ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ λόγος τοῦ πατρὸς ἐν ἰδέα καὶ ἐνεργείᾳ· πρὸς αὐτοῦ γὰρ καὶ δι᾽ αὐτοῦ πάντα ἐγένετο, ἑνὸς ὄντος τοῦ πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ.
greek_edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. 7 (Athenagoras), Jena 1857; archive.org copy = Sandig reprint, Wiesbaden 1969 (metadata). Greek and Latin on facing pages; Greek apparatus with German/Latin notes. Read from text-layer PDF (Google scan, OCR) cross-checked by rendered page images. Printed pp. 44 (end: ἔστιν ὃ υἱὸς, text layer) and 46 (main text). CONFLICT: Otto main text as read on scan reads 'ἐν ἰδέα'; Otto's own apparatus note 19 and Migne PG 6 read 'ἐν ἰδέᾳ'. Greek here follows Otto's main text.
english: But the Son of God is the Logos of the Father, in idea and in operation; for after the pattern of Him and by Him were all things made, the Father and the Son being one.
page: Otto p. 46 (Greek main text); ANF page unknown
edition: B. P. Pratten, in Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Co.; year not checked). Read from newadvent.org text.
what_it_says: The Son is the Logos of the Father 'in idea and in operation', and all things were made through Him, the Father and Son being one.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (oneness of Father and Son); also a hard passage: 'idea' and 'operation' are modal/functional, which Arians and modalists both cite
limits: Does not give the Son an 'essence' of the same kind as the Father; ἰδέα/ἐνέργεια contrast reads as ideal vs real principle (Otto notes 19-20). Pratten's 'in idea and in operation' is the ANF rendering.

greek: Ὄντος δὲ τοῦ υἱοῦ ἐν πατρὶ καὶ πατρὸς ἐν υἱῷ, ἑνότητι καὶ δυνάμει πνεύματος, νοῦς καὶ λόγος τοῦ πατρὸς ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ. Εἰ δὲ δι᾽ ὑπερβολὴν συνέσεως σκοπεῖν ὑμῖν ἔπεισιν, ὁ παῖς τί βούλεται, ἐρῶ διὰ βραχέων·
greek_edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. 7 (Athenagoras), Jena 1857; archive.org copy = Sandig reprint, Wiesbaden 1969 (metadata). Greek and Latin on facing pages; Greek apparatus with German/Latin notes. Read from text-layer PDF (Google scan, OCR) cross-checked by rendered page images. Printed p. 46 (PDF 131) with apparatus note 9 (p. 46) on 'πνεύματος'. Migne PG 6 agrees word for word ('νοῦς καὶ Λόγος τοῦ Πατρὸς, ὁ Υἱὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ').
english: And, the Son being in the Father and the Father in the Son, in oneness and power of spirit, the understanding and reason (νοῦς καὶ λόγος) of the Father is the Son of God. But if, in your surpassing intelligence, it occurs to you to inquire what is meant by the Son,
edition: B. P. Pratten, in Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Co.; year not checked). Read from newadvent.org text.
what_it_says: The Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son by oneness and power of 'spirit'; the Father's νοῦς and λόγος is the Son of God.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (mutual indwelling = perichoresis-like). Answer to objection: 'power of spirit' can be read as the divine essence, not the Holy Spirit as a person (Otto note 9)
limits: 'πνεύματος' here, per Otto note 9 (citing Clericus, Maranus, Dorner), probably means the common divine essence, not the Holy Spirit as a person. Opponents (Unitarian) read the phrase as a modal unity. 'νοῦς καὶ λόγος' is identified with the Son in the same sentence.

greek: Εἰ δὲ δι᾽ ὑπερβολὴν συνέσεως σκοπεῖν ὑμῖν ἔπεισιν, ὁ παῖς τί βούλεται, ἐρῶ διὰ βραχέων· πρῶτον γέννημα εἶναι τῷ πατρί, οὐχ ὡς γενόμενον (ἐξ ἀρχῆς γὰρ ὁ θεὸς, νοῦς ἀΐδιος ὤν, εἶχεν αὐτὸς ἐν ἑαυτῷ τὸν λόγον, ἀϊδίως λογικὸς ὤν),
greek_edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. 7 (Athenagoras), Jena 1857; archive.org copy = Sandig reprint, Wiesbaden 1969 (metadata). Greek and Latin on facing pages; Greek apparatus with German/Latin notes. Read from text-layer PDF (Google scan, OCR) cross-checked by rendered page images. Printed p. 46 (PDF 131). Migne PG 6 agrees except 'ὧν' (same word as Otto 'ὤν').
english: I will state briefly that He is the first product of the Father, not as having been brought into existence (for from the beginning, God, who is the eternal mind [νοῦς], had the Logos in Himself, being from eternity instinct with Logos [λογικός]);
edition: B. P. Pratten, in Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Co.; year not checked). Read from newadvent.org text.
what_it_says: The Son is the Father's first product (πρῶτον γέννημα), not something that came to be; God was eternal mind with the Logos in Himself from the beginning.
use: hard passage: supports Arian-looking 'first product' language; the answer is the immediate qualification 'οὐχ ὡς γενόμενον' and 'ἀΐδιος', i.e. the Logos is eternal as λόγος in God
limits: The text does not say 'eternal Son' in these words. 'γέννημα' is a 'product/offspring' term that Arians cited; Otto's note 10 records only a manuscript variant on γενόμενον, not on πρῶτον. How the eternal Logos relates to the 'coming forth' remains open in this chapter.

greek: ἀλλ᾽ ὡς τῶν ὑλικῶν ξυμπάντων, ἀποίου φύσεως καὶ γῆς ἀχρείας ὑποκειμένων δίκην, μεμιγμένων τῶν παχυμερεστέρων πρὸς τὰ κουφότερα ἐπ᾽ αὐτοῖς, ἰδέα καὶ ἐνέργεια εἶναι προελθών.
greek_edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. 7 (Athenagoras), Jena 1857; archive.org copy = Sandig reprint, Wiesbaden 1969 (metadata). Greek and Latin on facing pages; Greek apparatus with German/Latin notes. Read from text-layer PDF (Google scan, OCR) cross-checked by rendered page images. Printed p. 46 (PDF 131). Variants (Otto note 12): γῆς ἀχρείας (scan) vs Migne γῆς ὀχείας; Otto's apparatus lists Fabricius προεῖλθον, and Migne has 'ἰδέα χαὶ ἐνέργεια εἶναι προελθών'.
english: but inasmuch as He came forth to be the idea and energizing power of all material things, which lay like a nature without attributes, and an inactive earth, the grosser particles being mixed up with the lighter.
edition: B. P. Pratten, in Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Co.; year not checked). Read from newadvent.org text.
what_it_says: The Logos 'came forth' (προελθών) to be the idea and energizing power of pre-existing unformed matter.
use: hard passage (answer): 'came forth' is not 'became'; the Logos is the form/pattern and power over matter. Supports the reading that 'comes forth' concerns creation (prophorikos), not a generation in time
limits: Otto's note 12 (German) says the Logos is 'nur hervorgegangen' (only come forth) and not 'erst Gewordenes'; the matter in the image is pre-existing and uncreated; whether critics read this as a non-Nicene dualism was not checked in this run.

greek: Καίτοι καὶ αὐτὸ τὸ ἐνεργοῦν τοῖς ἐκφωνοῦσι προφητικῶς ἅγιον πνεῦμα ἀπόῤῥοιαν εἶναί φαμεν τοῦ θεοῦ, ἀποῤῥέον καὶ ἐπαναφερόμενον ὡς ἀκτῖνα ἡλίου.
greek_edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. 7 (Athenagoras), Jena 1857; archive.org copy = Sandig reprint, Wiesbaden 1969 (metadata). Greek and Latin on facing pages; Greek apparatus with German/Latin notes. Read from text-layer PDF (Google scan, OCR) cross-checked by rendered page images. Printed p. 48 (PDF 133). Apparatus note 14 (same page): Bodl. 1.2 'καὶ ἀπόῤῥδοιαν'; Lübker's order 'ἀπόῤῥοιαν φαμὲν τοῦ θεοῦ εἶναι'. Migne PG 6 'ἀπόῤῥοιαν εἶναί φαμεν τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἀποῤῥέον καὶ ἐπαναφερόμενον'.
english: The Holy Spirit Himself also, which operates in the prophets, we assert to be an effluence of God, flowing from Him, and returning back again like a beam of the sun.
edition: B. P. Pratten, in Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Co.; year not checked). Read from newadvent.org text.
what_it_says: The Holy Spirit, which works in the prophets, is an effluence (ἀπόῤῥοια) of God that flows out and returns, like a ray of the sun.
use: objection (Sabellian/modalist and some 'Spirit is only power' readers cite the ray image); also answers the question 'person or power?' only partly
limits: ἀπόρροια and ἀκτὶς ἡλίου are impersonal images; the text does not say the Spirit is a hypostasis/person. Migne and Otto agree on the Greek. Otto's apparatus is silent on personhood. Compare Leg. 10 'ἐνεργοῦν' = operates.

greek: Συνάδει δὲ τῷ λόγῳ καὶ τὸ προφητικὸν πνεῦμα· Κύριος γάρ, φησίν, ἔκτισέ με ἀρχὴν ὁδῶν αὐτοῦ εἰς ἔργα αὐτοῦ. Καίτοι καὶ αὐτὸ τὸ ἐνεργοῦν τοῖς ἐκφωνοῦσι προφητικῶς ἅγιον πνεῦμα ἀπόῤῥοιαν εἶναί φαμεν τοῦ θεοῦ, ἀποῤῥέον καὶ ἐπαναφερόμενον ὡς ἀκτῖνα ἡλίου.
greek_edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. 7 (Athenagoras), Jena 1857; archive.org copy = Sandig reprint, Wiesbaden 1969 (metadata). Greek and Latin on facing pages; Greek apparatus with German/Latin notes. Read from text-layer PDF (Google scan, OCR) cross-checked by rendered page images. Printed pp. 46-48 (PDF 131, 133). Otto note 48: 'Prov. 8, 22'; variants 'ἔκτισέ με'/'εἰ κύριος'. Migne PG 6 agrees.
english: The prophetic Spirit also agrees with our statements. The Lord, it says, made me, the beginning of His ways to His works. Proverbs 8:22
edition: B. P. Pratten, in Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Co.; year not checked). Read from newadvent.org text.
what_it_says: Athenagoras cites Prov. 8:22 ('the Lord made me') as the prophetic witness to the Logos, then turns to the Spirit as 'effluence'.
use: hard passage: Prov. 8:22 'ἔκτισέ με' is the classic Arian proof-text (creation of the Son); Athenagoras uses it for the Logos before creation
limits: Athenagoras does not explain the verb; the Arian reading 'created' is the one he avoids with 'not as having been made' (A2-05). Otto note 48 records that Justin also read this verse of the Logos.

greek: Τίς οὖν οὐκ ἂν ἀπορήσαι, λέγοντας ϑεὸν πατέρα καὶ υἱὸν ϑεὸν καὶ πνεῦμα ἅγιον, δεικνύντας αὐτῶν καὶ τὴν ἐν τῇ ἑνώσει δύναμιν καὶ τὴν ἐν τῇ τάξει διαίρεσιν, ἀκούσας ἀθέους καλουμένους;
greek_edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. 7 (Athenagoras), Jena 1857; archive.org copy = Sandig reprint, Wiesbaden 1969 (metadata). Greek and Latin on facing pages; Greek apparatus with German/Latin notes. Read from text-layer PDF (Google scan, OCR) cross-checked by rendered page images. Printed p. 48 (PDF 133). Migne PG 6 agrees.
english: Who, then, would not be astonished to hear men who speak of God the Father, and of God the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and who declare both their power in union and their distinction in order, called atheists?
edition: B. P. Pratten, in Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Co.; year not checked). Read from newadvent.org text.
what_it_says: Athenagoras says that Christians who name God the Father, God the Son and the Holy Spirit, and show their power in unity and distinction in rank, are wrongly called atheists.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (the earliest explicit Father-Son-Spirit triad in the Legatio together with unity 'ἑνώσει' and 'τάξει' distinction)
limits: 'τάξις' (rank/order) and 'ἑνώσις' (union) are not the Nicene vocabulary (no ὁμοούσιος, no Τριάς, checked in ch. 10). Opponents: ordering = subordination; defenders: 'ἐν τῇ τάξει' is ordering of manifestation, not nature (Otto: 'ihrer Stellung nach').

ref: Leg. 10.4-5 (Otto ch. 10 close, into 10.5 end at p. 50)
greek: Καὶ οὐκ ἐπὶ τούτοις τὸ ϑεολογικὸν ἡμῶν ἵσταται μέρος· ἀλλὰ καὶ πλῆθος ἀγγέλων καὶ λειτουργῶν φαμεν, οὓς ὁ ποιητὴς καὶ δημιουργὸς κόσμου θεὸς διὰ τοῦ παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ λόγου διένειμε καὶ διέταξε περί τε τὰ στοιχεῖα εἶναι καὶ τοὺς οὐρανοὺς καὶ τὸν κόσμον καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτῷ καὶ τὴν τούτων εὐταξίαν.
greek_edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. 7 (Athenagoras), Jena 1857; archive.org copy = Sandig reprint, Wiesbaden 1969 (metadata). Greek and Latin on facing pages; Greek apparatus with German/Latin notes. Read from text-layer PDF (Google scan, OCR) cross-checked by rendered page images. Printed pp. 48-50 (PDF 133, 135). Migne PG 6 reads 'κόσμου Θεὸς' (genitive); the scan glyph is hard to read at 600 dpi (κόσμου/κόσμον). Otto text layer: 'καὶ τοὺς οὐρανοὺς'.
english: Nor is our teaching in what relates to the divine nature confined to these points; but we recognise also a multitude of angels and ministers, whom God the Maker and Framer of the world distributed and appointed to their several posts by His Logos, to occupy themselves about the elements, and the heavens, and the world, and the things in it, and the goodly ordering of them all.
edition: B. P. Pratten, in Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Co.; year not checked). Read from newadvent.org text.
what_it_says: Besides the Father, Son and Spirit, Christians acknowledge angels and ministers, created and distributed by God through His Logos to govern the elements and heavens.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (the Logos is the agent through which God orders creation; the angels are distinct, created ministers, so the Son is not one of them)
limits: The Son is not called an angel here; 'ὑπηρέτης' does not occur in ch. 10 (checked). Angels are 'λειτουργοί' (ministers), not the Logos. Angels as created intermediaries are a point Unitarians cite in Athenagoras's cosmology.

greek: 9. ἑνότητι καὶ δυνάμει πνεύματος] Hic πνεύματος nomine non persona spiritus sancti sed spiritualis essentia patris et filii (1. Clericus Histor. eccl. duorum prim. saeculorum, Amst. 1716, p. 705) i.e. divinitas (Maran.), das gemeinsame göttliche Wesen (I. A. Dorner ... 1845, p. 210) significatur
greek_edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. 7 (Athenagoras), Jena 1857; archive.org copy = Sandig reprint, Wiesbaden 1969 (metadata). Greek and Latin on facing pages; Greek apparatus with German/Latin notes. Read from text-layer PDF (Google scan, OCR) cross-checked by rendered page images. Apparatus note 9 on printed p. 46 (PDF 131). Latin/German note text, read from text layer and checked on the rendered page.
english: Own translation (from the Latin): 'Here the name of the spirit does not mean the person of the Holy Spirit but the spiritual essence of the Father and the Son ... i.e. divinity (Maranus), the common divine being (Dorner).'
edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. 7 (Athenagoras), Jena 1857; archive.org copy = Sandig reprint, Wiesbaden 1969 (metadata). Greek and Latin on facing pages; Greek apparatus with German/Latin notes. Read from text-layer PDF (Google scan, OCR) cross-checked by rendered page images.
what_it_says: Otto's commentary takes 'power of spirit' (πνεύματος) as the common divine essence, not the Holy Spirit as a person.
use: answer to objection: a Unitarian reading of the Spirit as 'power' is supported by a 19th-century editor's commentary, so the Trinitarian reader cannot take this clause as a personal Spirit by itself
limits: A scholarly gloss, not Athenagoras's text. Defenders of the Nicene reading (Bull, Newman, per the brief's list) were not checked here; the note is one editor's argument, not a consensus.

greek: 19. ἐν ἰδέᾳ (im idealen Sinne) ... 20. ἐν ἐνεργείᾳ (im realen Sinne)
greek_edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. 7 (Athenagoras), Jena 1857; archive.org copy = Sandig reprint, Wiesbaden 1969 (metadata). Greek and Latin on facing pages; Greek apparatus with German/Latin notes. Read from text-layer PDF (Google scan, OCR) cross-checked by rendered page images. Notes 19 (printed p. 45, PDF 130) and 20 (printed p. 46, PDF 131). Note 19 is in the Latin page; lemma read from text layer.
english: Own translation: 'in idea' (in the ideal sense), 'in operation' (in the real sense); Otto glosses the pair as 'ideal and real principle of the world, archetype of all things and principle of their actuality'.
edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. 7 (Athenagoras), Jena 1857; archive.org copy = Sandig reprint, Wiesbaden 1969 (metadata). Greek and Latin on facing pages; Greek apparatus with German/Latin notes. Read from text-layer PDF (Google scan, OCR) cross-checked by rendered page images.
what_it_says: Otto reads 'idea' and 'operation' as the ideal and real principles of the world: the Logos is archetype and principle of actuality.
use: explanation of hard pass: 'in idea and in operation' is a metaphysical pair (pattern and power), not a claim about personhood; this is the defence most used against Arian 'instrument' readings
limits: Otto's gloss, not Athenagoras's words. Modalists (Sabellians) can read the same pair as two modes of one God; the Nicene defender must add the 'Son of God' title and the 'first product' clause.

greek: ἔστιν ὁ Υἱὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ Λόγος τοῦ Πατρὸς ἐν ἰδέᾳ καὶ ἐνεργείᾳ. Πρὸς αὐτοῦ γὰρ καὶ δι᾽ αὐτοῦ πάντα ἐγένετο, ἑνὸς ὄντος τοῦ Πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ Υἱοῦ.
greek_edition: Migne, Patrologia Graeca vol. 6 (Paris 1857), text from archive.org item patrologiae_cursus_completus_gr_vol_006_justin_et_al_version1 (djvu text; the PDF is 83 MB, over the 60 MB limit, so not downloaded). Printed as ἐν ἰδέᾳ, with footnote (66) in the Migne text.
page: PG 6, col. 909 (inferred: running header '910' falls before 'ἑνὸς ὄντος'; column not confirmed on scan)
what_it_says: Same sentence as A2-03; Migne prints 'ἐν ἰδέᾳ' (with ᾳ), which Otto's apparatus also reads.
limits: Only the Greek text layer was read; no page image was checked. The ἰδέα/ἰδέᾳ point decides whether Otto's main text has a typo; the sense is unchanged.

greek: ϑεοῦ, λόγος τοῦ πατρός, ἐν ἰδέᾳ etc. In Bodl. 1. 2 voci λόγος articulus ὁ praecedit, eundemque Fr. Lücke ... et Gieseler ... receperunt. Sed non opus est.
greek_edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. 7 (Athenagoras), Jena 1857; archive.org copy = Sandig reprint, Wiesbaden 1969 (metadata). Greek and Latin on facing pages; Greek apparatus with German/Latin notes. Read from text-layer PDF (Google scan, OCR) cross-checked by rendered page images. Note 8 on printed p. 45 (PDF 130), text layer read; Latin/German commentary.
english: Own translation of the note's point: editors other than Maranus punctuate badly ('θεοῦ, λόγος τοῦ πατρός, ἐν ἰδέᾳ'); two manuscripts add the article 'ὁ' before λόγος (Lücke, Gieseler adopt it); Otto says it is not necessary.
edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. 7 (Athenagoras), Jena 1857; archive.org copy = Sandig reprint, Wiesbaden 1969 (metadata). Greek and Latin on facing pages; Greek apparatus with German/Latin notes. Read from text-layer PDF (Google scan, OCR) cross-checked by rendered page images.
what_it_says: Otto records a textual variant: whether the Son is 'ὁ λόγος' (with article) or 'λόγος'; he keeps the text without the article.
use: answer to objection: the article question is not decisive; the 'λόγος' with or without article does not change the sense of 'Son of God is the Logos'
limits: Textual point only; the Son-Logos identity is in the text either way. Otto decides against the article, Lücke and Gieseler for it.

greek: ἀπόῤῥοιαν)] Bodl. 1. 2. Act. καὶ ἀπόῤῥδοιαν. Lüb. alio ordine: ἀπόῤῥοιαν φαμὲν τοῦ θεοῦ εἶναι.
greek_edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. 7 (Athenagoras), Jena 1857; archive.org copy = Sandig reprint, Wiesbaden 1969 (metadata). Greek and Latin on facing pages; Greek apparatus with German/Latin notes. Read from text-layer PDF (Google scan, OCR) cross-checked by rendered page images. Note 14 on printed p. 48 (PDF 133). Text-layer OCR; not checked letter by letter.
english: Own translation: 'ἀπόῤῥοιαν' — manuscripts Bodl. 1 and 2 and Actus give 'καὶ ἀπόῤῥδοιαν'; Lübker gives the other word order 'ἀπόῤῥοιαν φαμὲν τοῦ θεοῦ εἶναι'.
edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. 7 (Athenagoras), Jena 1857; archive.org copy = Sandig reprint, Wiesbaden 1969 (metadata). Greek and Latin on facing pages; Greek apparatus with German/Latin notes. Read from text-layer PDF (Google scan, OCR) cross-checked by rendered page images.
what_it_says: The manuscript and editorial variants for ἀπόρροια do not change its sense (effluence of God); the word itself is secure.
use: answer to objection: the key term for the Spirit is attested in the manuscripts, so the 'effluence' image is not an editorial invention
limits: Variant readings are OCR-read; the ἀπόρροια word is in every witness listed, but the spelling ἀπόῤῥοια with rough breathing and ῤ is an Otto convention.
